subfield: Plasma physics / laser-plasma interaction and accelerator physics
motivation: Tajima (with the late John Dawson) showed in 1979 that an intense laser pulse can drive a plasma wake whose electric fields exceed those of conventional accelerators by three orders of magnitude. Turning this idea into reality required deep understanding of nonlinear, kinetic plasma physics. Malka's group, and Leemans's in parallel, demonstrated quasi-monoenergetic electron beams in 2004. Leemans then used plasma channel guiding to reach multi-GeV energies over centimetre distances. Laser wakefield acceleration is now an established field. It provides compact sources of femtosecond electron bunches and betatron X-rays, has driven free-electron lasing, and holds promise for future colliders and for medical and industrial uses. This is a rare case where elegant plasma theory, persistent experiment and laser technology came together to create a new way of accelerating particles, which has reshaped plasma and accelerator physics worldwide.
